summary: This Part II develops the finite, odd-characteristic representation theory needed by tame and classical p-adic types. Starting from the parent roadmap’s algebraic Heisenberg extension, it constructs Schrödinger models, proves central-character uniqueness including cyclic centers of higher p-power order, and normalizes a genuine finite symplectic action. Partial-polarization restriction retains the quadratic determinant twist, and isotropic induction and tensor fixed vectors supply the finite inputs to Fintzen and Stevens. The independent automorphic theta-correspondence routes have an explicit companion-roadmap proposal.

nodes.title: Adapted finite symplectic coordinates
nodes.statement: For every isotropic subspace I≤V, assemble finite Schrödinger coordinates V=I⊕V₀⊕J with I⊥=I⊕V₀, perfect I–J pairing and nondegenerate V₀. The coordinate equivalence identifies the form with B₀ orthogonally summed with B((x,y),(x′,y′))=y′(x)−y(x′) on I⊕I*. Its API records dim V=2 dim I+dim V₀. General adapted Lagrangian bases are imported from MordellLawrenceVenkatesh:LV.3/lagrangian-symplectic-basis; general symplectic-basis existence and even dimension already exist in current Tau Ceti and are not new targets. Use native Submodule, LinearEquiv and BilinForm; this target packages the specified partial decomposition for the finite models.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate.
I is isotropic: B vanishes on I×I.
proofSteps: Extend I to a maximal isotropic subspace L. A vector in L⊥ outside L would enlarge L isotropically, so L=L⊥; native orthogonal dimensions give dim V=2 dim L. Extend a basis of I to one of L.

Apply the imported Lagrangian basis-extension theorem to this chosen basis. Let J be spanned by the dual vectors paired with the basis of I; let V₀ be spanned by the remaining paired basis vectors. The symplectic-basis equations directly give the required orthogonal decomposition and I⊥=I⊕V₀.

Identify J with I* by y(x)=B(x,y). Read the dimension formula, the quotient identification and full polarizations from these coordinates. General basis existence, basis extension and even dimension retain their existing owners; no separate theorem for them is planned here.
acceptance: The complement to I in I⊥ is the quotient symplectic space, with its induced form.
No assertion is made that a fixed chosen complement is preserved by its parabolic stabilizer.

For a full polarization, reuse the imported Lagrangian basis-extension theorem. Current TauCeti LinearMap.BilinForm.IsAlt.exists_basis_toMatrix_eq_J and even_finrank are comparisons after the pin, not pinned baseline citations.

nodes.title: Finite Schrödinger representation
nodes.statement: For a full polarization V=X⊕X*, construct the native FDRep Sψ of H(V) on Fun(X,C), by (π(t,x,y)f)(z)=ψ(t+y(z)+y(x)/2)f(z+x). Supply a linear equivalence with native induction from A={(t,0,y)} of its character (t,0,y)↦ψ(t). Here induction is realized as functions F(ah)=ψ(tₐ)F(h), with H acting by right translation; restriction to representatives (0,x,0) fixes the coordinate convention. Its dimension is |X|=qⁿ.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
A full polarization has been chosen.
proofSteps: Use the imported bilinear factor-set multiplication and the displayed formula to check π(h)π(h′)=π(hh′): the two cross terms differ by B(v,v′)/2. Inverses give invertible operators.

Linearity and finite X bundle the operators into an FDRep. For functions F(ah)=ψ(tₐ)F(h), set f(z)=F((0,z,0)); right translation by (t,x,y) has subgroup factor (t+y(z)+y(x)/2,0,y), giving the displayed formula. Use TauCeti.Rep.indSubtypeEquivPi_ρ_apply and the existing induction–coinduction comparison to identify this with native induction.
A delta-function basis identifies dimension with |X|. Central action is ψ(t), translations are z↦z+x, and modulations are multiplication by ψ(y(z)).

nodes.title: Finite Schrödinger character
nodes.statement: The character of Sψ at (t,v) is qⁿψ(t) if v=0 and is 0 otherwise. Thus its normalized character norm is 1. This holds for every nontrivial additive character of any finite odd field, including characters with a nontrivial additive kernel.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
proofSteps: For x≠0, translation has no fixed basis vector, so the diagonal trace is zero. For x=0, sum ψ(t+y(z)) over X; a nonzero functional y is onto k and primitive-character orthogonality makes this sum zero.
For v=0 the scalar action gives qⁿψ(t). Sum χ(h)χ(h⁻¹) over the q-element center, divide by |H|=q^(2n+1), and get 1. The order follows from the imported extension equivalence with k×V.
acceptance: The test must distinguish nontrivial from faithful ψ over F₉; nonzero y is detected by a suitable scalar multiple even when ψ(y(z))=1 for one z.

sources.match: The character is concentrated on the center; its norm and completeness are then computed.

nodes.title: Finite Stone–von Neumann theorem
nodes.statement: Sψ is irreducible. Every irreducible complex representation of H(V) on which (t,0) acts as ψ(t) is isomorphic to Sψ; it has dimension qⁿ and scalar endomorphisms. In an arbitrary finite-dimensional representation with this central action, every irreducible constituent is Sψ, so it is Sψ-isotypic.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
proofSteps: Apply the native character-norm criterion to the preceding character. For another simple representation with this central character, pair its character with that of Sψ: only the center contributes and the pairing equals dim(A)/qⁿ, a positive number. Native orthogonality forces an isomorphism.
Maschke decomposes any finite-dimensional representation into simples, each with the prescribed scalar central action. Native Schur gives scalar endomorphisms.

Uniqueness is an isomorphism class, not a distinguished nonzero vector or a uniquely normalized intertwiner.

nodes.title: Stone–von Neumann with a cyclic center
nodes.statement: Let J be a finite group, H normal in J, J/H abelian, and θ:H→Cˣ invariant under conjugation by J. Assume that for each g∉H there is x∈J with θ(gxg⁻¹x⁻¹)≠1. Then there is exactly one isomorphism class of irreducible η with η(h)=θ(h)·id. Its dimension d satisfies d²=[J:H], and its character is dθ on H and zero off H. Every representation containing θ is η-isotypic on its θ-isotypic J-subrepresentation. In the routed application J is a finite p-group, p odd, J/H is an Fp-vector space with nondegenerate θ-commutator pairing; H/ker θ can have order pᵃ. No exponent-p or standard-Heisenberg-isomorphism hypothesis is needed.
hypotheses: J is finite; H is normal; every commutator lies in H.
θ is J-invariant and its commutator radical in J/H is zero.
All representations are complex and finite-dimensional.
proofSteps: Induce the existing one-dimensional θ representation from H. J-invariance implies its H action is scalar θ; it is nonzero by its positive dimension. Maschke supplies a nonzero simple constituent η.

For g∉H choose x detecting its commutator. Since commutators act scalarly, conjugating η(g) multiplies its trace by the nontrivial scalar θ([g,x]) (or its inverse, according to the conjugation direction), so the trace vanishes.

Character norm of a simple η is |H|d²/|J|=1, hence d²=[J:H]. Pair any two such simple representations: the same calculation gives 1, and character orthogonality yields an isomorphism. Decompose the θ-isotypic subrepresentation by Maschke.
acceptance: Test a central product of the order-p³ standard Heisenberg group with C_(p²), identifying their order-p central subgroups: the faithful cyclic central character has one representation of dimension p.
The nonabelian group of order p³ and exponent p² is also covered; it need not admit a special isomorphism to the exponent-p standard group.
If the commutator pairing is degenerate, uniqueness can fail: an abelian J with H proper has many extensions of a fixed H-character.

nodes.title: Intertwiners between finite polarizations
nodes.statement: For Lagrangians A,B≤V let S_A be functions F:H→C with F((t,a)h)=ψ(t)F(h) for a∈A, acted on by right translation. Define T_BA:S_A→S_B by (T_BA F)(h)=∑_(b∈B)F((0,b)h). It is a nonzero H-intertwiner and an isomorphism. With this unnormalized convention, T_AA=|A|id and T_AB∘T_BA=|A|·|A∩B|id. These are chosen intertwiners, not an assertion that all triple compositions are exactly 1.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
A and B are Lagrangian.
proofSteps: Use the imported Heisenberg product and isotropy of B to reindex the B sum, proving its left covariance; right translation commutes with left averaging.
Apply T_BA to the function supported on the inducing subgroup of A; its value at 1 is |A∩B|, hence it is nonzero. Stone–von Neumann makes it an isomorphism.
For the composite, sum ψ of the commutator character on the finite quotient; character orthogonality leaves |A|·|A∩B|. Equal Lagrangians give |A|id directly.
acceptance: Every sum is a finite sum; no Haar measure or local-field topology is imported.

nodes.title: Determinant normalization of the Weil action
nodes.statement: Let Rf(z)=f(−z), S⁺=ker(R−1), S⁻=ker(R+1). Their dimensions are (qⁿ+1)/2 and (qⁿ−1)/2. Every μ(g) commutes with R. Put κ(g)=det μ(g)/(det(μ(g)|S⁺))² and ω(g)=κ(g)μ(g). Then ω:Sp(V)→GL_C(Sψ) is a genuine homomorphism with Egorov covariance, independent of the chosen scalar representatives μ. It is characterized among scalar corrections by det ω(g)=(det(ω(g)|S⁺))². This specifies a preferred action even for Sp₂(F₃), where arbitrary linearizations are not unique.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
proofSteps: Parity implements the central symplectic element −1. Its conjugate by μ(g) is a scalar multiple of R by Schur. As trace R=1, conjugacy invariance of trace makes this scalar 1.
Decompose functions into even and odd parts using 1/2. The only fixed point of z↦−z is 0, giving the dimensions and dim S−2 dim S⁺=−1.
For μ(g)μ(g′)=c μ(gg′), determinants give κ(g)κ(g′)=c⁻¹κ(gg′). Thus the corrected operators multiply exactly. Rescaling μ by a multiplies κ by a⁻¹; the normalized action is independent of choices.
Apply the same exponent −1 to any two scalar corrections satisfying the determinant condition to prove uniqueness of this preferred normalization.
acceptance: A proof that uses perfectness of every finite symplectic group fails at Sp₂(F₃); the determinant proof must handle it directly.

sources.match: The ratio of determinants on the whole space and its even subspace removes the projective multiplier.

For u(C), pair z and −z in the determinant to obtain κ=1. For m(A), the even-subspace permutation determinant squares to 1, so the ratio is the sign of the permutation z↦A⁻¹z on all of X. This is χ_k(det A): elementary transvections have odd order and sign +1; a diagonal scaling reduces to its permutation of k, whose sign is its quadratic character since kˣ is cyclic. The other coordinates repeat this permutation an odd number of times.

For J use the displayed determinant ratio, which requires no unproved choice of Gauss-sum square root. Finite Fourier inversion gives Fψ²=R. The preferred normalization then yields the formulas and their relations.
acceptance: For q=3,n=1, ψ(1)=exp(2πi/3), obtain ω(u(1))=diag(1,ζ,ζ), ω(m(−1))=−R and κ_J=−i.
For q=5,n=1, ψ(1)=exp(2πi/5), κ_J=−1 and ω(m(2))δ₀=−δ₀.
Retain κ_J as a determinant formula; no local Weil index or analytic Gauss-sum evaluation is a prerequisite.

nodes.title: Weil–Heisenberg semidirect representation
nodes.statement: On the native semidirect product H(V)⋊Sp(V), with (h,g)(h′,g′)=(h(g·h′),gg′), define Ω(h,g)=π(h)ω(g). This is a genuine complex FDRep. Its restriction to H(V) is Sψ, its restriction to Sp(V) is the normalized Weil action, and its center acts by ψ. Transport along isometries is compatible up to the unique scalar ambiguity of the underlying Heisenberg intertwiner; the transported normalized symplectic action is exact after conjugation.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
proofSteps: Use the parent isometry action to form the existing native SemidirectProduct; no new group carrier is needed.
Insert Egorov into π(h)ω(g)π(h′)ω(g′) to obtain π(h(g·h′))ω(gg′). Bundle the finite-dimensional representation.
Conjugate both π and ω by a nonzero Heisenberg intertwiner. The determinant characterization is preserved under conjugation, so the resulting normalized action agrees.
acceptance: The representation is genuine on a finite semidirect product; no local metaplectic double cover is introduced.

nodes.title: Transport through compatible special coordinates
nodes.statement: Let P be an abstract finite group with a specified isomorphism j:P≃H(V) inducing the given identification P/Z(P)≃V and its given central character. Let K act on P, let s:K→Sp(V), and require j(k·a)=s(k)·j(a) for every k,a. Then (a,k)↦(j(a),s(k)) is a homomorphism P⋊K→H(V)⋊Sp(V), and its pullback of Ω is a genuine extension of the Heisenberg representation to P⋊K. Merely having a special isomorphism on quotients, or an arbitrary center-fixing action, does not imply this equivariance hypothesis.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
j is a group isomorphism with the stated center and quotient identifications.
s is a homomorphism and the displayed equivariance is part of the input.
proofSteps: Check the native semidirect multiplication using precisely the equivariance assumption, then restrict the representation along the resulting homomorphism.
Central action and the representation on P follow from j; the K action follows from s. Changing j compatibly conjugates the pulled-back action.
Do not manufacture j from nondegeneracy alone. Cyclic-center groups of order pᵃ and exponent-p² groups are handled by the separate uniqueness theorem, without a false standard-group identification.
acceptance: An inner translation in Aut_Z(P) generally adds a nonzero central linear term in j coordinates, and is not a pure symplectic action under this fixed j.

nodes.title: Partial-polarization induced model
nodes.statement: For an adapted decomposition V=I⊕V₀⊕J, let K=H(I⊥)=H(I⊕V₀). Projection K→H(V₀) has kernel I={(0,i)}. Inflate Sψ,₀ along this projection. Then Sψ,V≅Ind_K^H(V)(Sψ,₀), with mixed realization Fun(J,Sψ,₀). Using representatives (0,j), the action of i∈I on the value at j is multiplication by ψ(B(j,i)), and its fixed vectors are exactly the functions supported at 0. Evaluation at 0 identifies Sψ,V^I with Sψ,₀, of dimension q^(dim V₀/2). Use native induction and native representation invariants.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
I is isotropic and adapted coordinates have been chosen.
proofSteps: Use the parent half-form product: the projection K→H(V₀) is a homomorphism and its kernel is I, because I pairs trivially with I⊥.
The native induced representation has the right central character and dimension |J|q^(dim V₀/2)=qⁿ. Stone–von Neumann and Maschke make it the unique Sψ,V, with multiplicity one.

Evaluate the induced functions on representatives (0,j). The identity (0,j)(0,i)=(B(j,i),i)(0,j) gives the multiplier ψ(B(j,i)). Nondegeneracy and primitivity show that only j=0 has trivial I-character. Evaluation and zero extension are inverse on fixed vectors.
acceptance: The fixed subspace has the smaller Heisenberg action; its parabolic action still requires the next determinant-character theorem.

nodes.title: Parabolic fixed-space representation
nodes.statement: Let P≤Sp(V) stabilize I. It acts on I and on V̄=I⊥/I, giving p₁:P→GL(I) and p₂:P→Sp(V̄). There is an isomorphism of P⋉H(V̄)-representations Sψ,V^I≅(χ_k∘det∘p₁)⊗Ωψ,V̄, where Ω is pulled back along p₂ on P and the identity on H(V̄). The H(V̄) action is obtained from H(I⊥)/I; an adapted complement identifies V̄ with V₀ but need not be P-stable.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
I is isotropic; P is its full stabilizer or any subgroup of that stabilizer.
proofSteps: The mixed-model evaluation identifies the smaller Heisenberg action. For the Levi subgroup GL(I)×Sp(V₀), the generator formulas give χ_k(det on I) times the smaller normalized Weil action.

In adapted coordinates, the parabolic unipotent radical has p₂=1. Its quadratic and mixed phases evaluate to 1 at the zero I-coordinate, so it acts trivially on the fixed subspace. This can be checked on the symmetric shear and off-diagonal generators of that radical.

Combine the Levi and radical actions and express the result intrinsically through p₁,p₂. This proves independence of the adapted complement and includes the determinant correction in Fintzen’s footnote.
acceptance: For V the F₅ plane and I its y-axis, m(2) acts on I by 2⁻¹=3 and on the fixed δ₀ line by χ₅(3)=−1. Equivalently choose I the x-axis and its constant-function line, where χ₅(2)=−1. These refer to the standard Schrödinger coordinates; the mixed model uses its own zero-support coordinate.
For I=0 the character is trivial and the result is Ωψ,V.
For I Lagrangian the fixed subspace is one-dimensional and its entire P action is χ_k(det p₁).

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 7.10, p. 33, especially footnote 3

nodes.title: Corrected Gérardin induction formula
nodes.statement: With P,I,V̄ as above, set Q=P⋉H(I⊥)≤P⋉H(V), using the same normal-first convention when formalizing. Inflate (χ_k∘det p₁)⊗Ωψ,V̄ to Q via H(I⊥)→H(V̄). Then Ωψ,V restricted to P⋉H(V) is isomorphic to Ind_Q^(P⋉H(V)) of that inflated representation. Its index factor is q^(dim I); the output dimension is qⁿ. The quadratic determinant factor is part of the inducing representation.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
P stabilizes the isotropic I.
proofSteps: Use the fixed subspace as a Q-subrepresentation of Sψ,V. Its H(I⊥) action factors through H(V̄), and its P action is the preceding formula.
Finite Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero map from induction to Ωψ,V. Its image is stable under H(V); irreducibility of Sψ,V makes the map surjective.
Native induction dimension is q^(dim I)q^(dim V̄/2)=qⁿ, so the map is an isomorphism. This recovers the corrected induction formula without relying on an unread proof.
acceptance: Dimension and restriction to the smaller Heisenberg subgroup must both agree.
A formula omitting χ_k(det p₁) fails the F₅ Lagrangian test.

nodes.title: Isotropic induction for cyclic-center quotients
nodes.statement: Assume the cyclic-center theorem data, now with J/H an Fp-vector space and θ([−,−])=ψ(B(−,−)) for nondegenerate alternating B and nontrivial ψ:Fp→Cˣ. Let I be isotropic, Q the inverse image of I⊥ in J, and U≤J map isomorphically onto I under J→J/H (more generally its kernel U∩H is allowed if θ is trivial there). Put H_I=HU and θ_I(hu)=θ(h). Then θ_I is a well-defined Q-invariant character; Q/H_I≅I⊥/I has the nondegenerate induced pairing. Let η_I be its unique irreducible representation. There are isomorphisms Ind_Q^J η_I≅η and η^U≅η_I as Q-representations; dim η_I=p^(dim(I⊥/I)/2). The invariant subspace is Q-stable because commutators [Q,U] lie in ker θ, even when U itself is not normal in Q.
hypotheses: J,H,θ satisfy the cyclic-center theorem, and the θ-commutator pairing is as stated over Fp.
U is a subgroup mapping onto I and θ is trivial on U∩H.
proofSteps: For h∈H,u∈U, J-invariance of θ and triviality on U∩H show that θ_I is well-defined and multiplicative. Orthogonality I⊥ makes it Q-invariant. Compute its radical as H_I using the nondegeneracy of the quotient form.
Apply cyclic-center Stone–von Neumann to Q,H_I,θ_I. Its induction to J has central H-character θ and dimension [J:Q]p^(dim(I⊥/I)/2)=p^(dim(J/H)/2), so isotypy makes it exactly η.

In the induced coset model indexed by J/Q, U acts on the identity coset trivially and on every other coset through a nontrivial character detected by the pairing. Thus only the identity coset contributes U-fixed vectors, giving η_I.
acceptance: For I=0 take U⊂H with θ(U)=1: Q=J and η_I=η.
For a Lagrangian I, Q=H_I and η_I is the line θ_I; induction has dimension pⁿ.
An isotropic quotient does not itself guarantee existence of a subgroup U with θ(U∩H)=1; that splitting is an explicit input supplied by the p-adic owner.

nodes.title: Iterated fixed line for unipotent actions
nodes.statement: Let I≤V be isotropic and U≤P=Stab(I). Suppose p₂(U) stabilizes a Lagrangian L₀≤V̄=I⊥/I. Let L be the inverse image of L₀ in I⊥, so L is Lagrangian in V. The line Sψ,V^L is U-stable and U acts on it by χ_k(det(u|I))χ_k(det(p₂(u)|L₀)). If both determinants are squares for every u∈U, this line is pointwise fixed and contains a nonzero U-fixed vector. In particular this holds when the two induced actions are unipotent. Apply this finite statement factor by factor to the plus-space and smaller Lagrangian in Fintzen’s Lemma 7.10.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of odd characteristic p, with q elements; representations have coefficients C.
V is finite-dimensional over k; B is alternating and nondegenerate; dim(V)=2n.
ψ:k→Cˣ is a nontrivial additive character. It need not be faithful if k is not a prime field.
U stabilizes I and its quotient action stabilizes L₀.
For the fixed-vector conclusion, both displayed determinant characters are trivial; unipotence is a sufficient condition.
proofSteps: Apply the parabolic fixed-space theorem to I, then to the Lagrangian L₀ of its quotient. The remaining Heisenberg space is zero, so its module is a line.
The two determinant twists multiply. Equivalently the filtration 0⊂I⊂L gives det(u|L)=det(u|I)det(p₂(u)|L₀).
Unipotent matrices have determinant 1, and quadraticChar(1)=1. A nonzero vector in this one-dimensional space is therefore fixed. This avoids false small-rank claims about commutator subgroups of GL.
acceptance: With V₀=0 the second determinant is the determinant on a zero-dimensional space, hence 1.
If a nonsquare scalar acts on I in an F₅ plane, the line is stable but has eigenvalue −1, so invariance cannot be concluded.
For I=0 the result is the standard fixed line attached to a U-stable Lagrangian.

nodes.title: Tensor compatibility and finite-type exports
nodes.statement: For an orthogonal sum V=⊥ᵢVᵢ and a single ψ, pull Sψ,V back along ∏ᵢH(Vᵢ)→H(V), (tᵢ,vᵢ)↦(∑tᵢ,∑vᵢ). It is isomorphic to ⊗ᵢSψ,Vᵢ; central tuples with ∑tᵢ=0 act trivially. Under ∏ᵢSp(Vᵢ)→Sp(V), this isomorphism intertwines the normalized Weil actions, and hence the Weil–Heisenberg actions. For any group U acting through these symplectic factors, nonzero fixed vectors vᵢ supplied by the preceding theorem have a nonzero U-fixed pure tensor. Dimensions multiply to q^(∑ᵢdim Vᵢ/2); the empty family is the one-dimensional trivial symplectic module. Together with cyclic-center uniqueness and isotropic induction, these are the finite inputs exported to the tame-type and classical-type roadmaps.
hypotheses: The family is finite, every Vᵢ is a finite nondegenerate odd-field symplectic space, and ψ is common to the factors.
Each U action factors through ∏Sp(Vᵢ), and each chosen vᵢ is nonzero and U-fixed.
proofSteps: In product Schrödinger coordinates Fun(∏Xᵢ,C) is the native tensor product of the finite function spaces; evaluate pure tensors by multiplying their values. This directly intertwines the Heisenberg action. Alternatively apply Stone–von Neumann and the dimension formula.

For two factors, the even subspace of the tensor product is S₁⁺⊗S₂⁺ ⊕ S₁⁻⊗S₂⁻. The determinant of the candidate ω₁⊗ω₂ satisfies the preferred determinant relation because dim Sᵢ⁺−dim Sᵢ⁻=1. Uniqueness of the parity normalization gives tensor compatibility even in the F₃ exception; induct on the family.
The tensor action fixes the pure tensor. Choose linear functionals ℓᵢ with ℓᵢ(vᵢ)=1; their tensor product evaluates it to 1, proving nonvanishing. Treat the empty family as the monoidal unit.
Export only these finite statements. The p-adic consumers prove their own filtration quotients, equivariant special coordinates, subgroup splittings, and identification of κ-factors.
acceptance: Two F₃ planes have a nine-dimensional tensor model and one fixed tensor line for the product of their standard unipotent subgroups.
No finite-quotient construction for a p-adic group is claimed here.
Central characters in the product must agree with the sum map on centers; independent incompatible ψᵢ cannot be collapsed through that map.
